compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same batch of supplies, the same list, the same three-day window, the same authority. If only one person is the site lead, their different access or authority may explain what they do.

| The same event (one batch, one list, equal authority) | ENFP: the basis more likely attended to | ISTJ: the basis more likely attended to | Which axis this row mainly sits on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional community relief project, two volunteers arrive early at the warehouse. One opens boxes and sets out labels. The other stacks supplies by district. The organisers can count on both of them for those tasks. Their reliability does not reveal their personality type.

The resemblance does not come from shared letters — not one matches — but from two things: the same set of four process names, and an externally visible willingness to pitch in. The first is a way of writing the stack; the second has far more to do with duty, experience and condition that day, and diligence cannot separate preferences.

The difference sits on all four axes. On E/I, the ENFP side turns attention and energy outward more often, so what is happening on the ground enters the field of view first; the ISTJ side more often returns to a framework already sorted out and then answers outward. That is direction, not who is more eager. On S/N, ENFP more often takes connections and possibility first, ISTJ more often observable facts and past experience. On T/F, ENFP more often puts people and values into the judgement, ISTJ more often relies on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently. On J/P, ISTJ more often forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward, ENFP more often keeps options and adjusts to new information.

All four differ, so this pair has no "shared letter" to treat as a default. Read the axes one at a time, and resist packing them into "one is flexible, one is rigid".

### Someone not on the list: serve first or check first

The distribution point is a small square. A woman arrives with a rent agreement, saying her child has just transferred schools and her household is not yet on the community list. Assume both have the same level of authority, the same stock, no supervisor on site that day, and both know that a missing registration has to be recorded afterwards — only with equal conditions is a comparison possible.

In this fictional scenario, both volunteers can ask what the decision would mean for the family and which eligibility rules apply to every household. The same authorisation limits both volunteers. If they need approval, either can contact the designated person and record the outcome. These are two considerations for one decision, not procedures assigned by type.

Each approach has a cost, and the cost is about authority and information at the time, not preference. Serving first may open a door, and the next day a group arrives saying they too were missed; checking first may leave one household waiting a day or two, and in the end relying on neighbours.

Order is not the criterion. An ENFP who has run distributions for years more often checks first, because they know the donor's accounts have to balance; an ISTJ on their first shift may push a pack across and sort the process out later. Role, duty, experience and conditions rewrite the order, and a single reaction cannot define a person.

Keep the counterexamples. Faced with someone visibly freezing, where the situation will not wait, ISTJ may hand the items over and complete the process afterwards; ENFP may design the receipt form in more detail than anyone, down to a field for the relationship of whoever collects on another's behalf. These only show that both types can do both things; they do not show which process was called on, or what anyone's function order is.

A workable exercise is to lay out the checking process rather than watch who moves first. Ask who set the form and the stock plan, who authorised the flexible packs, and who has to approve an exception; then have both write three "situations where an exception can be made on the spot" with reasons, and swap. If both wrote infants, people living alone and damaged housing, the disagreement may only be about how tight the process is; if one wrote "no exceptions", what needs discussing is the scope of authority and where responsibility sits, not type. The comparison is only for finding standards, authority or information that need negotiating.

Where the site involves safety judgements such as electric heaters or gas equipment, preference does not decide: follow local electricity, gas and fire service guidance and seek help if needed; the two people are only responsible for stating and recording what has been confirmed.

### Why the four parts match and the whole thing inverts

Line the two writings up vertically: ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si, ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. The first row meets the fourth, the second meets the third, and no part is missing.

In the model, the inversion means the emphases are exactly offset: ENFP more often unfolds possibilities first, ISTJ more often matches against what has already happened. But that describes emphasis in preference only; it does not say who finds the work harder, who needs reminding, or who cannot do it. A position is a description inside the model, and does not predict ability or explain the psychological cause of one action.

The offset is often described as mutual irritation and mutual need: one may find the other "making it up as they go", the other may find them "only accepting what is already written down". A position is a division of labour inside the model, not a sequence of actions; in practice ENFP will also prepare the forms in advance, and ISTJ will also change a plan on the spot.

On the attitude of the third process, the common writing labels ENFP's Te extraverted and ISTJ's Fi introverted, while other sources give only the function name without settling the direction. Where versions disagree, check which source it cites, then read the first two positions for this pair. Both full pages are the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Volunteers can name two distinct tasks: following up with households missing from the list and reconciling the distribution records. They can assign either task based on authority, experience and availability.

### Two hundred packs: who opens the exception, who guards the account

(Fictional scene.) Three districts, two hundred packs, and the lists for two of the districts were put together three days ago in a hurry; both have the same authorisation note. One approach is to walk the furthest district to see who actually lives there — newly moved tenants, couples doing temporary work on building sites, people mostly absent from the list; this person also more often sets aside a reserve. The other sorts the two hundred packs by district and household number, gives each household a receipt slip, reconciles the total at the end of the day and traces any shortfall immediately. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, authority and available information.

Keeping only a reserve without keeping accounts may end with totals that cannot be explained when the donor asks; keeping only accounts without a reserve may mean shaking your head at someone outside the list, and the atmosphere on site turns stiff. Both costs come from process design, not from anyone's character.

A workable move is to write the reserve into the process: hold twenty packs back, record each one drawn, who approved it, who received it and why. The exception stays open and the account stays intact. Who owns which stretch is decided by who knows how, who has the authority and who is present that day, not by type; when the people change, the division should change with them.

### A cousin filling in university applications: talk about the life first, or the score table

(Fictional scene.) A cousin has to submit university choices, the family is in the living room, and the scores, region and admissions rules are already on the table. One approach asks what he enjoys, whether he could accept studying away from home, and what kind of life he pictures; it also names a few directions that do not look like the standard answer and lets him choose. The other works through the score bands of the past three years, where graduates of each programme go, and the admission rules item by item, crossing out what is clearly out of reach. Either approach can be used by the same person, and the order depends on the task and the information available.

The one who talks about wishes may worry the child gets boxed in by a score and spends four years in a subject that never engages him; the one who reads scores may worry that after a long conversation the score turns out not to reach. Both concerns are legitimate, and the difference is which kind of information is put on the table first.

The counterexamples are equally clear: ISTJ may make several calls to students already on a programme to understand what it is really like; ENFP may copy the historical scores of every shortlisted institution into a notebook. Such behaviour shows both approaches are within range for both people, and cannot be turned around to prove anyone's function order.

The student can check published entry requirements, note where admission is uncertain and compare the programmes they want to study. Past scores can inform an estimate when they are relevant, but do not by themselves determine which options are open.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is "ENFP sees many possibilities, so has no direction". Seeing many possibilities is the normal state of this writing and has nothing to do with whether the work has method; ENFP can be very steady inside a familiar process, only the steadiness usually comes from leaving room rather than writing the steps in stone.

The second is "ISTJ relies on existing facts, so is stuck in the past". Reliance on established facts is often an advantage with supplies, accounts and records; ISTJ also adopts new methods, only they more often need the problem with the old one stated first.

The third is "all four letters differ, so they are nothing alike". This pair shares all four process names in a different order; reading only the letters suggests no common language, and reading only the function names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth is treating E as "likes socialising". In the preferences E means attention and energy turn outward more often; both types may want to speak to nobody after a long day, and both may organise a roomful of people when it is needed.

The fifth is treating "who serves first, who checks first" as the criterion. What happens first is shaped by role, duty, experience and conditions, and the same type makes different choices on different days; sequence carries no classificatory value.

The resemblance does not come from shared letters — not one matches — but from two things: the same set of four process names, and an externally visible willingness to pitch in. The first is a way of writing the stack; the second has far more to do with duty, experience and condition that day, and diligence cannot separate preferences.

The difference sits on all four axes. On E/I, the ENFP side turns attention and energy outward more often, so what is happening on the ground enters the field of view first; the ISTJ side more often returns to a framework already sorted out and then answers outward. That is direction, not who is more eager. On S/N, ENFP more often takes connections and possibility first, ISTJ more often observable facts and past experience. On T/F, ENFP more often puts people and values into the judgement, ISTJ more often relies on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently. On J/P, ISTJ more often forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward, ENFP more often keeps options and adjusts to new information.
All four differ, so this pair has no "shared letter" to treat as a default. Read the axes one at a time, and resist packing them into "one is flexible, one is rigid".
### Someone not on the list: serve first or check first

The distribution point is a small square. A woman arrives with a rent agreement, saying her child has just transferred schools and her household is not yet on the community list. Assume both have the same level of authority, the same stock, no supervisor on site that day, and both know that a missing registration has to be recorded afterwards — only with equal conditions is a comparison possible.

In this fictional scenario, both volunteers can ask what the decision would mean for the family and which eligibility rules apply to every household. The same authorisation limits both volunteers. If they need approval, either can contact the designated person and record the outcome. These are two considerations for one decision, not procedures assigned by type.

Each approach has a cost, and the cost is about authority and information at the time, not preference. Serving first may open a door, and the next day a group arrives saying they too were missed; checking first may leave one household waiting a day or two, and in the end relying on neighbours.

Order is not the criterion. An ENFP who has run distributions for years more often checks first, because they know the donor's accounts have to balance; an ISTJ on their first shift may push a pack across and sort the process out later. Role, duty, experience and conditions rewrite the order, and a single reaction cannot define a person.

Keep the counterexamples. Faced with someone visibly freezing, where the situation will not wait, ISTJ may hand the items over and complete the process afterwards; ENFP may design the receipt form in more detail than anyone, down to a field for the relationship of whoever collects on another's behalf. These only show that both types can do both things; they do not show which process was called on, or what anyone's function order is.

A workable exercise is to lay out the checking process rather than watch who moves first. Ask who set the form and the stock plan, who authorised the flexible packs, and who has to approve an exception; then have both write three "situations where an exception can be made on the spot" with reasons, and swap. If both wrote infants, people living alone and damaged housing, the disagreement may only be about how tight the process is; if one wrote "no exceptions", what needs discussing is the scope of authority and where responsibility sits, not type. The comparison is only for finding standards, authority or information that need negotiating.

Where the site involves safety judgements such as electric heaters or gas equipment, preference does not decide: follow local electricity, gas and fire service guidance and seek help if needed; the two people are only responsible for stating and recording what has been confirmed.
### Why the four parts match and the whole thing inverts
Line the two writings up vertically: ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si, ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. The first row meets the fourth, the second meets the third, and no part is missing.

In the model, the inversion means the emphases are exactly offset: ENFP more often unfolds possibilities first, ISTJ more often matches against what has already happened. But that describes emphasis in preference only; it does not say who finds the work harder, who needs reminding, or who cannot do it. A position is a description inside the model, and does not predict ability or explain the psychological cause of one action.

The offset is often described as mutual irritation and mutual need: one may find the other "making it up as they go", the other may find them "only accepting what is already written down". A position is a division of labour inside the model, not a sequence of actions; in practice ENFP will also prepare the forms in advance, and ISTJ will also change a plan on the spot.

On the attitude of the third process, the common writing labels ENFP's Te extraverted and ISTJ's Fi introverted, while other sources give only the function name without settling the direction. Where versions disagree, check which source it cites, then read the first two positions for this pair. Both full pages are the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

body: Volunteers can name two distinct tasks: following up with households missing from the list and reconciling the distribution records. They can assign either task based on authority, experience and availability.
### Two hundred packs: who opens the exception, who guards the account

(Fictional scene.) Three districts, two hundred packs, and the lists for two of the districts were put together three days ago in a hurry; both have the same authorisation note. One approach is to walk the furthest district to see who actually lives there — newly moved tenants, couples doing temporary work on building sites, people mostly absent from the list; this person also more often sets aside a reserve. The other sorts the two hundred packs by district and household number, gives each household a receipt slip, reconciles the total at the end of the day and traces any shortfall immediately. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, authority and available information.

Keeping only a reserve without keeping accounts may end with totals that cannot be explained when the donor asks; keeping only accounts without a reserve may mean shaking your head at someone outside the list, and the atmosphere on site turns stiff. Both costs come from process design, not from anyone's character.

A workable move is to write the reserve into the process: hold twenty packs back, record each one drawn, who approved it, who received it and why. The exception stays open and the account stays intact. Who owns which stretch is decided by who knows how, who has the authority and who is present that day, not by type; when the people change, the division should change with them.
### A cousin filling in university applications: talk about the life first, or the score table

(Fictional scene.) A cousin has to submit university choices, the family is in the living room, and the scores, region and admissions rules are already on the table. One approach asks what he enjoys, whether he could accept studying away from home, and what kind of life he pictures; it also names a few directions that do not look like the standard answer and lets him choose. The other works through the score bands of the past three years, where graduates of each programme go, and the admission rules item by item, crossing out what is clearly out of reach. Either approach can be used by the same person, and the order depends on the task and the information available.

The one who talks about wishes may worry the child gets boxed in by a score and spends four years in a subject that never engages him; the one who reads scores may worry that after a long conversation the score turns out not to reach. Both concerns are legitimate, and the difference is which kind of information is put on the table first.

The counterexamples are equally clear: ISTJ may make several calls to students already on a programme to understand what it is really like; ENFP may copy the historical scores of every shortlisted institution into a notebook. Such behaviour shows both approaches are within range for both people, and cannot be turned around to prove anyone's function order.

body: The first misread is "ENFP sees many possibilities, so has no direction". Seeing many possibilities is the normal state of this writing and has nothing to do with whether the work has method; ENFP can be very steady inside a familiar process, only the steadiness usually comes from leaving room rather than writing the steps in stone.

The second is "ISTJ relies on existing facts, so is stuck in the past". Reliance on established facts is often an advantage with supplies, accounts and records; ISTJ also adopts new methods, only they more often need the problem with the old one stated first.

The third is "all four letters differ, so they are nothing alike". This pair shares all four process names in a different order; reading only the letters suggests no common language, and reading only the function names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth is treating E as "likes socialising". In the preferences E means attention and energy turn outward more often; both types may want to speak to nobody after a long day, and both may organise a roomful of people when it is needed.

The fifth is treating "who serves first, who checks first" as the criterion. What happens first is shaped by role, duty, experience and conditions, and the same type makes different choices on different days; sequence carries no classificatory value.

body: When earlier and later results differ, check whether the same item bank, version, language and scoring convention were used, then which kind of experience you were referring to: projects at work, or matters at home. Circumstances push answers toward one side, but one score cannot establish a stable tendency, and the result should not be read backwards into "I must have acted first".

Put the practice in everyday scenes with similar roles and comparable conditions: pick a few recent occasions when the list or the information in hand was incomplete, and write a few lines for each — what information you had, what authority you held, on what grounds you finally chose, and what would have changed the decision. Most often "being conscientious". Both may arrive early and carry boxes to the last trip, and diligence cannot separate them at all.

items.question: What is most often misread between ENFP and ISTJ?

items.answer:
In the exchange between the first and fourth positions. ENFP's first, Ne, is ISTJ's fourth, and ISTJ's first, Si, is ENFP's fourth; Fi and Te swap in the middle.

items.answer:
They are counterexamples to a stereotype, not evidence for a function order.

items.question: ISTJ makes an exception and ENFP reconciles the accounts — are those counterexamples?

items.answer:
Write "exception" and "reconciliation" as two parallel lines: one owns the reserve and the judgement about people outside the list, the other owns receipts and totals, and the two lines reconcile once before the day closes.

items.question: Distributing supplies: how do they divide the work without clashing?

items.answer:
Comments such as “stop making it up as you go” or “you can only follow the rules” can turn a disagreement about the work into a personal judgement. There is no basis here for saying which comment would upset someone more.

Reword it to the matter at hand: whether to keep a reserve this time, whether to check the list first this time, which line the exception goes on. Discussing the arrangement is far more useful than evaluating how the other person thinks.

body: In a fictional community relief project, two volunteers arrive early at the warehouse. One opens boxes and sets out labels. The other stacks supplies by district. The organisers can count on both of them for those tasks. Their reliability does not reveal their personality type.

The resemblance does not come from shared letters — not one matches — but from two things: the same set of four process names, and an externally visible willingness to pitch in. The first is a way of writing the stack; the second has far more to do with duty, experience and condition that day, and diligence cannot separate preferences.

The difference sits on all four axes. On E/I, the ENFP side turns attention and energy outward more often, so what is happening on the ground enters the field of view first; the ISTJ side more often returns to a framework already sorted out and then answers outward. That is direction, not who is more eager. On S/N, ENFP more often takes connections and possibility first, ISTJ more often observable facts and past experience. On T/F, ENFP more often puts people and values into the judgement, ISTJ more often relies on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently. On J/P, ISTJ more often forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward, ENFP more often keeps options and adjusts to new information.
All four differ, so this pair has no "shared letter" to treat as a default. Read the axes one at a time, and resist packing them into "one is flexible, one is rigid".
### Someone not on the list: serve first or check first

The distribution point is a small square. A woman arrives with a rent agreement, saying her child has just transferred schools and her household is not yet on the community list. Assume both have the same level of authority, the same stock, no supervisor on site that day, and both know that a missing registration has to be recorded afterwards — only with equal conditions is a comparison possible.

In this fictional scenario, both volunteers can ask what the decision would mean for the family and which eligibility rules apply to every household. The same authorisation limits both volunteers. If they need approval, either can contact the designated person and record the outcome. These are two considerations for one decision, not procedures assigned by type.

Each approach has a cost, and the cost is about authority and information at the time, not preference. Serving first may open a door, and the next day a group arrives saying they too were missed; checking first may leave one household waiting a day or two, and in the end relying on neighbours.

Order is not the criterion. An ENFP who has run distributions for years more often checks first, because they know the donor's accounts have to balance; an ISTJ on their first shift may push a pack across and sort the process out later. Role, duty, experience and conditions rewrite the order, and a single reaction cannot define a person.

Keep the counterexamples. Faced with someone visibly freezing, where the situation will not wait, ISTJ may hand the items over and complete the process afterwards; ENFP may design the receipt form in more detail than anyone, down to a field for the relationship of whoever collects on another's behalf. These only show that both types can do both things; they do not show which process was called on, or what anyone's function order is.

A workable exercise is to lay out the checking process rather than watch who moves first. Ask who set the form and the stock plan, who authorised the flexible packs, and who has to approve an exception; then have both write three "situations where an exception can be made on the spot" with reasons, and swap. If both wrote infants, people living alone and damaged housing, the disagreement may only be about how tight the process is; if one wrote "no exceptions", what needs discussing is the scope of authority and where responsibility sits, not type. The comparison is only for finding standards, authority or information that need negotiating.

Where the site involves safety judgements such as electric heaters or gas equipment, preference does not decide: follow local electricity, gas and fire service guidance and seek help if needed; the two people are only responsible for stating and recording what has been confirmed.
### Why the four parts match and the whole thing inverts
Line the two writings up vertically: ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si, ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. The first row meets the fourth, the second meets the third, and no part is missing.

In the model, the inversion means the emphases are exactly offset: ENFP more often unfolds possibilities first, ISTJ more often matches against what has already happened. But that describes emphasis in preference only; it does not say who finds the work harder, who needs reminding, or who cannot do it. A position is a description inside the model, and does not predict ability or explain the psychological cause of one action.

The offset is often described as mutual irritation and mutual need: one may find the other "making it up as they go", the other may find them "only accepting what is already written down". A position is a division of labour inside the model, not a sequence of actions; in practice ENFP will also prepare the forms in advance, and ISTJ will also change a plan on the spot.

On the attitude of the third process, the common writing labels ENFP's Te extraverted and ISTJ's Fi introverted, while other sources give only the function name without settling the direction. Where versions disagree, check which source it cites, then read the first two positions for this pair. Both full pages are the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

comparison_public_projection_v1.summary:
ENFP and ISTJ differ on all four MBTI preference pairs: Extraversion and Introversion, Intuition and Sensing, Feeling and Thinking, and Perceiving and Judging. These are differences in their four-letter codes. They do not imply opposite skills, values or behaviour.

- E/I: whether attention and energy turn more toward the outer world (E) or the inner one (I). This describes direction, not social skill and not how much someone talks.
- S/N: whether someone tends to give more weight to observable facts and experience (S) or to patterns, connections and possibilities (N).
- T/F: whether judgement rests on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently (T), or puts people and values into the judgement (F).
- J/P: whether outer life forms arrangements and conclusions first (J), or keeps options and adjusts to new information (P).

Applied to each type: ENFP's attention turns outward, sourcing leans to connections and possibility, judgement to people and values, and outer life to keeping options; ISTJ's attention turns inward, sourcing leans to facts and experience, judgement to impersonal consistency, and outer life to forming arrangements.

Using the type-dynamics convention on this page, the stacks are: Ne–Fi–Te–Si for ENFP and Si–Te–Fi–Ne for ISTJ. All four process names are present and the order is fully reversed: ENFP's dominant Ne is ISTJ's fourth position, ISTJ's dominant Si is ENFP's fourth, and Fi and Te swap in the middle. The attitude of the third process (Te for ENFP, Fi for ISTJ) is labelled differently elsewhere; this writing is a convention adopted here, not the Foundation's only version.

These describe emphasis inside the model. They do not predict the order of behaviour, rank ability, or say whether two people work well together or get along. In the winter distribution below, whether someone not on the list is served before or after being checked depends on the authority granted, the stock, the urgency at the time and who is on duty; four preference axes are not a typing rule.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a fictional community relief project, two volunteers arrive early at the warehouse. One opens boxes and sets out labels. The other stacks supplies by district. The organisers can count on both of them for those tasks. Their reliability does not reveal their personality type.

The resemblance does not come from shared letters — not one matches — but from two things: the same set of four process names, and an externally visible willingness to pitch in. The first is a way of writing the stack; the second has far more to do with duty, experience and condition that day, and diligence cannot separate preferences.

The difference sits on all four axes. On E/I, the ENFP side turns attention and energy outward more often, so what is happening on the ground enters the field of view first; the ISTJ side more often returns to a framework already sorted out and then answers outward. That is direction, not who is more eager. On S/N, ENFP more often takes connections and possibility first, ISTJ more often observable facts and past experience. On T/F, ENFP more often puts people and values into the judgement, ISTJ more often relies on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently. On J/P, ISTJ more often forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward, ENFP more often keeps options and adjusts to new information.

All four differ, so this pair has no "shared letter" to treat as a default. Read the axes one at a time, and resist packing them into "one is flexible, one is rigid".

### Someone not on the list: serve first or check first

The distribution point is a small square. A woman arrives with a rent agreement, saying her child has just transferred schools and her household is not yet on the community list. Assume both have the same level of authority, the same stock, no supervisor on site that day, and both know that a missing registration has to be recorded afterwards — only with equal conditions is a comparison possible.

In this fictional scenario, both volunteers can ask what the decision would mean for the family and which eligibility rules apply to every household. The same authorisation limits both volunteers. If they need approval, either can contact the designated person and record the outcome. These are two considerations for one decision, not procedures assigned by type.

Each approach has a cost, and the cost is about authority and information at the time, not preference. Serving first may open a door, and the next day a group arrives saying they too were missed; checking first may leave one household waiting a day or two, and in the end relying on neighbours.

Order is not the criterion. An ENFP who has run distributions for years more often checks first, because they know the donor's accounts have to balance; an ISTJ on their first shift may push a pack across and sort the process out later. Role, duty, experience and conditions rewrite the order, and a single reaction cannot define a person.

Keep the counterexamples. Faced with someone visibly freezing, where the situation will not wait, ISTJ may hand the items over and complete the process afterwards; ENFP may design the receipt form in more detail than anyone, down to a field for the relationship of whoever collects on another's behalf. These only show that both types can do both things; they do not show which process was called on, or what anyone's function order is.

A workable exercise is to lay out the checking process rather than watch who moves first. Ask who set the form and the stock plan, who authorised the flexible packs, and who has to approve an exception; then have both write three "situations where an exception can be made on the spot" with reasons, and swap. If both wrote infants, people living alone and damaged housing, the disagreement may only be about how tight the process is; if one wrote "no exceptions", what needs discussing is the scope of authority and where responsibility sits, not type. The comparison is only for finding standards, authority or information that need negotiating.

Where the site involves safety judgements such as electric heaters or gas equipment, preference does not decide: follow local electricity, gas and fire service guidance and seek help if needed; the two people are only responsible for stating and recording what has been confirmed.

### Why the four parts match and the whole thing inverts

Line the two writings up vertically: ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si, ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. The first row meets the fourth, the second meets the third, and no part is missing.

In the model, the inversion means the emphases are exactly offset: ENFP more often unfolds possibilities first, ISTJ more often matches against what has already happened. But that describes emphasis in preference only; it does not say who finds the work harder, who needs reminding, or who cannot do it. A position is a description inside the model, and does not predict ability or explain the psychological cause of one action.

The offset is often described as mutual irritation and mutual need: one may find the other "making it up as they go", the other may find them "only accepting what is already written down". A position is a division of labour inside the model, not a sequence of actions; in practice ENFP will also prepare the forms in advance, and ISTJ will also change a plan on the spot.

On the attitude of the third process, the common writing labels ENFP's Te extraverted and ISTJ's Fi introverted, while other sources give only the function name without settling the direction. Where versions disagree, check which source it cites, then read the first two positions for this pair. Both full pages are the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

sections.body_md:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same batch of supplies, the same list, the same three-day window, the same authority. If only one person is the site lead, their different access or authority may explain what they do.

All six rows align situation, authority and deadline, and the last column names the preference axis. The table compares the basis for sourcing and judging, not speed, effort or reliability.

| The same event (one batch, one list, equal authority) | ENFP: the basis more likely attended to | ISTJ: the basis more likely attended to | Which axis this row mainly sits on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Getting oriented before the distribution starts | May clarify what needs doing by talking it through with the volunteers | May clarify the same tasks by reviewing the plan and reflecting privately | E/I: directing attention outward or inward. Either person can use both approaches. |
| Receiving the distribution list | What pattern in the same list could point to households missing from it | Which names, districts and totals can be matched to the same records | Sourcing preference, leaning S/N |
| Someone not on the list arrives | Weigh the household’s immediate needs among the options allowed by the same rules | Apply the same eligibility criteria to this household that would apply to any other | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Supplies run short | Which households could share one pack, and whether there is another way to split | Reorder by the agreed priority and household number, and notify people | Allocation and shared rules; either type can check |
| Whether to fix the finishing time now | Keep the finishing time open within the agreed limits until more is known | Agree on provisional finish and handover times and revise them if needed | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| How to judge it is finished | Weigh what remaining issues mean for the households affected | Apply the same completion criteria to the records for each district | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. An ENFP with five years of distributions reconciles accounts expertly, and an ISTJ on a first shift may hand over first and complete the process later; the same person also changes approach with the information they hold, their scope of authority and whether someone else has taken over, so these rows cannot be used to classify.
sections.title: ENFP and ISTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Volunteers can name two distinct tasks: following up with households missing from the list and reconciling the distribution records. They can assign either task based on authority, experience and availability.

### Two hundred packs: who opens the exception, who guards the account

(Fictional scene.) Three districts, two hundred packs, and the lists for two of the districts were put together three days ago in a hurry; both have the same authorisation note. One approach is to walk the furthest district to see who actually lives there — newly moved tenants, couples doing temporary work on building sites, people mostly absent from the list; this person also more often sets aside a reserve. The other sorts the two hundred packs by district and household number, gives each household a receipt slip, reconciles the total at the end of the day and traces any shortfall immediately. Both types can combine these bases; which step is taken depends on the division of work, authority and available information.

Keeping only a reserve without keeping accounts may end with totals that cannot be explained when the donor asks; keeping only accounts without a reserve may mean shaking your head at someone outside the list, and the atmosphere on site turns stiff. Both costs come from process design, not from anyone's character.

A workable move is to write the reserve into the process: hold twenty packs back, record each one drawn, who approved it, who received it and why. The exception stays open and the account stays intact. Who owns which stretch is decided by who knows how, who has the authority and who is present that day, not by type; when the people change, the division should change with them.

### A cousin filling in university applications: talk about the life first, or the score table

(Fictional scene.) A cousin has to submit university choices, the family is in the living room, and the scores, region and admissions rules are already on the table. One approach asks what he enjoys, whether he could accept studying away from home, and what kind of life he pictures; it also names a few directions that do not look like the standard answer and lets him choose. The other works through the score bands of the past three years, where graduates of each programme go, and the admission rules item by item, crossing out what is clearly out of reach. Either approach can be used by the same person, and the order depends on the task and the information available.

The one who talks about wishes may worry the child gets boxed in by a score and spends four years in a subject that never engages him; the one who reads scores may worry that after a long conversation the score turns out not to reach. Both concerns are legitimate, and the difference is which kind of information is put on the table first.

The counterexamples are equally clear: ISTJ may make several calls to students already on a programme to understand what it is really like; ENFP may copy the historical scores of every shortlisted institution into a notebook. Such behaviour shows both approaches are within range for both people, and cannot be turned around to prove anyone's function order.

The student can check published entry requirements, note where admission is uncertain and compare the programmes they want to study. Past scores can inform an estimate when they are relevant, but do not by themselves determine which options are open.
sections.title: ENFP and ISTJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
The first misread is "ENFP sees many possibilities, so has no direction". Seeing many possibilities is the normal state of this writing and has nothing to do with whether the work has method; ENFP can be very steady inside a familiar process, only the steadiness usually comes from leaving room rather than writing the steps in stone.

The second is "ISTJ relies on existing facts, so is stuck in the past". Reliance on established facts is often an advantage with supplies, accounts and records; ISTJ also adopts new methods, only they more often need the problem with the old one stated first.

The third is "all four letters differ, so they are nothing alike". This pair shares all four process names in a different order; reading only the letters suggests no common language, and reading only the function names suggests the two are the same.

The fourth is treating E as "likes socialising". In the preferences E means attention and energy turn outward more often; both types may want to speak to nobody after a long day, and both may organise a roomful of people when it is needed.

The fifth is treating "who serves first, who checks first" as the criterion. What happens first is shaped by role, duty, experience and conditions, and the same type makes different choices on different days; sequence carries no classificatory value.
sections.title: ENFP and ISTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When earlier and later results differ, check whether the same item bank, version, language and scoring convention were used, then which kind of experience you were referring to: projects at work, or matters at home. Circumstances push answers toward one side, but one score cannot establish a stable tendency, and the result should not be read backwards into "I must have acted first".

Put the practice in everyday scenes with similar roles and comparable conditions: pick a few recent occasions when the list or the information in hand was incomplete, and write a few lines for each — what information you had, what authority you held, on what grounds you finally chose, and what would have changed the decision. If "can this standard be applied consistently", "what does this mean for the people involved" and "settle it or look again" keep reappearing, they are worth discussing as your habit in sourcing and judging.

These notes are not voted on, set no threshold, and do not claim to settle more than a retest. If the item bank reports dimension scores, a score near the boundary only means that label is sensitive to changes in your answers; do not over-read it, and do not infer that you switch between two function orders.
sections.title: ENFP and ISTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Most often "being conscientious". Both may arrive early and carry boxes to the last trip, and diligence cannot separate them at all.

What to look at is not how committed they are but what the commitment more often draws on: one more often cites "who has still not been looked after", the other more often cites "whether every item reconciles". Both are called responsibility, and neither is evidence for a type.
items.question: What is most often misread between ENFP and ISTJ?

items.answer:
In the exchange between the first and fourth positions. ENFP's first, Ne, is ISTJ's fourth, and ISTJ's first, Si, is ENFP's fourth; Fi and Te swap in the middle.

Worth stating: positions describe emphasis in preference inside the model, do not predict ability, do not predict how effortful the work feels, and do not explain the psychological cause of one action. The two are not "missing an ability"; the same set of processes is used first more often from different seats.
items.question: The four function names match — where does the difference between ENFP and ISTJ sit?

items.answer:
They are counterexamples to a stereotype, not evidence for a function order.

Claims like "ISTJ never bends" and "ENFP cannot keep accounts" were never sound: whether someone does a thing depends on duty, training, scope of authority and willingness at the time, none of which relates to a function order. So these examples refute the impressions above, but cannot prove which process was called on or where it sits. To distinguish the two, look not at whether a step was added afterwards but at which kind of evidence is cited more often across comparable situations.
items.question: ISTJ makes an exception and ENFP reconciles the accounts — are those counterexamples?

items.answer:
Write "exception" and "reconciliation" as two parallel lines: one owns the reserve and the judgement about people outside the list, the other owns receipts and totals, and the two lines reconcile once before the day closes.

The key is to write the exception authority down: who approves, how many packs, where it is recorded. Once that is clear, an exception is part of the rules. Who takes which line depends on experience, authority and who is present that day, not on type.
items.question: Distributing supplies: how do they divide the work without clashing?

items.answer:
Comments such as “stop making it up as you go” or “you can only follow the rules” can turn a disagreement about the work into a personal judgement. There is no basis here for saying which comment would upset someone more.

Reword it to the matter at hand: whether to keep a reserve this time, whether to check the list first this time, which line the exception goes on. Discussing the arrangement is far more useful than evaluating how the other person thinks.
items.question: Working with an ENFP or an ISTJ, which sentence lands hardest?

items.answer:
Check the assessment name, version, language and scoring convention, and confirm both used the same questionnaire; then which kind of experience you were referring to — projects at work, or matters at home. Circumstances push answers toward one side, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at which of the four sits closer to the boundary; sitting near a boundary only means that label is sensitive to changes in your answers, not that two complete types both hold, and it does not imply switching between stacks. Without dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer a boundary and no retest interval is prescribed.

Framework sources: the preference definitions follow the [official Myers-Briggs facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's account of type dynamics processes](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

Four-position convention: the arrangement on this page, especially the attitude of the third process (Te for ENFP, Fi for ISTJ), is the common writing adopted here and is an editorial convention; sources handle it differently, and this writing is not presented as the Foundation's only version, nor used to predict the order of behaviour, level of ability or whether two people get along.

Editorial fiction: the winter distribution, the two hundred packs and the cousin's applications are all editorial composites, corresponding to no real project, family or person, written only to practise discrimination, and constituting no distribution standard, safety guidance or education advice.

Scope limits: assessment results are not for ranking ability, screening candidates or predicting relationships. The FermatMind assessment uses its own item bank and scoring; the scope is set out in the [scoring and evidence note](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
